newsitem.title: MEXICO: Disaffected Mexico leftist finally gets his chance.
newsitem.headline: Disaffected Mexico leftist finally gets his chance.

text.p: He was raised in the presidential palace and combines two of the most potent names in Mexican history, but until this year Cuauhtemoc Cardenas seemed doomed to failure.

After two unsuccessful presidential challenges and the near-collapse of the left-wing party he founded after quitting the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) in 1987, Cardenas' political obituaries were being written last year.

Now the 63-year-old disaffected former PRI senator, famous for his dour face and wooden speeches, has won a chance to govern the heart of Mexico's huge capital, according to exit polls from Sunday's elections.
The mayor's position will provide Cardenas a national forum for his left-wing views.

Supporters saw his victory as a vindication of the man who many Mexicans believe was cheated out of the presidency in 1988 by a massive electoral fraud. Opponents moaned about what they term his old-style PRI mentality and outdated opinions.
Commentators see his three-year Mexico City mayor's term as a springboard for a likely third presidential challenge in 2000 but Cardenas played down this possibility during the campaign.
Instead, he pledged to change the lives of the 17 million inhabitants of this sprawling, polluted, crime-ridden city.
His Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) would "push our agenda for a more social face to economic policy" he said last week. "That is what our party is all about".

The son of Mexico's most popular president this century, Lazaro Cardenas, Cuauhtemoc was born in the capital on May 1, 1934 at the start of his father's six-year term. He began his career like dozens of other well-connected PRI politicians -- making the most of a powerful surname.

After earning an engineering degree from Mexico's National Autonomous University (UNAM) -- even today, his supporters refer to him respectfully as "The Engineer" -- Cardenas held various jobs overseeing dam projects until winning election as a PRI senator in 1976.
Months later he became a deputy minister and in 1980 was elected governor of his family's home state of Michoacan, a largely rural province in western Mexico.

Analysts said his name -- Cuauhtemoc was the heroic last Aztec emperor, defeated with his army in a sea of blood by invading Spaniards in 1521 -- and his Indian looks were big assets with Mexico's poor.
Cardenas stirred controversy during his six-year governor's term by transferring a large stretch of Michoacan's Pacific coast beach from the state to his mother for a token sum.

Asked about the incident during this year's election campaign, Cardenas said the land previously belonged to an aunt who gave it to the state to sort out legal problems and had always intended that it be passed eventually to his mother.

Opponents also charged that Cardenas piled up a large fortune during his political career with the PRI, but "The Engineer" always denied any wrongdoing. His declaration of income this year included an apartment in Madrid and various properties in Mexico.
Cardenas shot to international fame in 1987, when he and a group of allies dramatically broke with the PRI to found their own movement, the National Democratic Front.

Cardenas ran for the presidency under the Front's colours in 1988 and won enormous support from PRI-weary Mexicans. First returns showed him way ahead of the PRI's Carlos Salinas de Gortari but then the results computer crashed.
When it came back up, Salinas had won the election.
Faced with protests about the result, the government denied wrongdoing but later burned the ballots to prevent a recount.
Salinas won huge popularity during his 1988-94 term of office as Cardenas's PRD crashed from defeat to defeat.

But the tables were turned once Salinas left office. His economic miracle vanished with the disastrous peso crash of December 1994 and the arrest of his brother Raul on murder charges in March 1995 appeared to confirm all that Cardenas and other opponents had alleged about high-level corruption.
Today, with a disgraced Salinas in self-imposed exile in Ireland and Cardenas triumphant in the Mexican capital, the roles of outcast and governor have finally been reversed.
